title: IPO Base
teaches: The IPO base as we trade it: a new issue's first rest under its own IPO high, light volume on the pullbacks, never bought on the listing day or in the listing week, the buy is the trade through the IPO high at market in regular hours and no more than 4% past it, the stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

steps: KRMN, 2025. Listed in February, it rests under its IPO high of 57.32 for 6.8 weeks, 22% deep, in a hot theme.

steps: VIK, 2024. Listed in May, it rests only 2.0 weeks under its IPO high, just 9% deep. The shallow end.
Short and tight is fine for a new issue. IBD wants light volume on the pullbacks, heavy on the way up.
2024-06-28: it clears the IPO high on 2.8x volume. Buy at market, 33.38. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 32.62.
Failure mode: stopped within days. Instead 3R comes in 10 days, then 5R. It rolls over after: the trail matters.

walkthroughs.title: MA, January 2007: the textbook stop-out
steps: MA, 2007. A 6.6-week, 17% base at the IPO high; the breakout hits 1.6x volume and closes near the high.
2007-01-17: buy 10.96. Stop 10.41, 5.0% away. The size came from that stop, so the loss is already planned.
The next session, 2007-01-18, trades down to 10.18 and takes the stop. Best 0.0R. We take the loss and move on.
The stock later ran for years. The rule is a probability, not a promise. A new buy needs a new trigger.

questions.q: What is an IPO base?
choices: A rest under a ten-year-old record high
A new issue's first rest under its high
A bounce up off the listing-day low
A spike that doubles in a few weeks
questions.answer: A new issue's first rest under its high
questions.why: A new issue's first rest under its high. IBD: let the stock build some trading history, then wait for its first base.
questions.lesson_line: An IPO base is a young stock's first rest under its own post-listing high.

wrong.A rest under a ten-year-old record high: That is an old stock's regular base. An IPO base belongs to a young stock and its own post-listing high.
wrong.A bounce up off the listing-day low: That is a bounce from the bottom. The base sits under the high, near the top of the range.
wrong.A spike that doubles in a few weeks: That is a pole. The base is the rest that comes after the early run.

questions.q: We can buy an IPO breakout on its listing day.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Never buy on the listing day or in the listing week. MarketSmith India says the same: not on the day, not in the week of listing.
questions.lesson_line: No buys on the listing day or in the listing week. Let the first heated days pass.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The pivot of an IPO base is the highest ___ since listing.
questions.answer: high
questions.why: High. The pivot is the left-side high, the IPO high. IBD adds 10 cents to it; with a market order the 10 cents does not matter.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the IPO high: the highest high since listing.

questions.q: The buy is a market order, placed once price trades through the IPO high in regular hours.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Price trades above the IPO high in regular hours, and entries are market orders. No buys outside regular hours.
questions.lesson_line: Trade through the IPO high, regular hours, market order.

questions.q: Where does the stop go on an IPO base breakout?
choices: A few cents under the IPO price
A few cents under the day's low
Exactly on the breakout day's low
A few cents under the base low
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the breakout day's low. The prior day's low is the other default. Not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the day's low, never at the base low.

wrong.A few cents under the IPO price: That is a level to watch, not our stop. The stop comes from the breakout day's low.
wrong.Exactly on the breakout day's low: A stop exactly on the low gets hit by the first wiggle. We sit a few cents under it.
wrong.A few cents under the base low: The base low can be far away. Widening the stop to sit through the base's depth is a named mistake.

questions.q: When the market stumbles into a correction, new issues often pull back the hardest.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. IBD says it is often the new issues that pull back the hardest. Buying in a weak market is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: New issues are sold first when the market weakens. Respect the market reading.

questions.q: In a healthy IPO base, volume is light on the pullbacks and heavy on the up days.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. IBD wants quiet action during declines and heavy volume on the upside. On the right half, up-day volume beats down-day volume.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet on the way down, busy on the way up. That is accumulation.

questions.q: Is this resting zone an IPO base?
choices: No, it must hold the listing-day low
Yes, the first rest under the high
No, it needs a rising 200-day first
questions.answer: Yes, the first rest under the high
questions.why: Yes. The top is the stock's own highest high since listing and nothing has closed above it. IBD says to wait for the first base.
questions.lesson_line: A young stock has no 200-day. The IPO high is its reference.

wrong.No, it must hold the listing-day low: The listing-day low is a level to watch. The base is the rest under the high, not a bounce off the low.
wrong.No, it needs a rising 200-day first: A young listing has no 200-day yet. That is why this card uses the IPO high instead.

questions.story: A stock listed six weeks ago. Its highest high came in week two. It has rested under that high for four weeks, 12% deep. Its low holds above the IPO price, and nothing has closed above the high.

questions.q: How long do IPO bases usually run, per IBD?
choices: Three to six months
Two to five weeks
Under a week
questions.answer: Two to five weeks
questions.why: Two to five weeks. IBD adds that in rare cases they can be as short as seven days.
questions.lesson_line: IPO bases run short: usually two to five weeks, not months.

wrong.Three to six months: That is a regular base on a seasoned stock. IBD says IPO bases run shorter.
wrong.Under a week: That is a pause, not a base. IBD's shortest rare case is seven days.

questions.q: A healthy IPO base ends with its last close in the top half of its range.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The base's last close sits in the top half of its range. A base still hugging its lows is not ready.
questions.lesson_line: The right side should be back in the top half of the range.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The IPO AVWAP is the volume-weighted average price anchored at the ___ day.
questions.answer: listing
questions.why: Listing. The IPO AVWAP is the volume-weighted average price anchored at the listing day.
questions.lesson_line: The IPO AVWAP starts counting on the listing day.

questions.q: Where does IBD put the buy point on an IPO base?
choices: 10 cents over the left-side high
At the bottom of the base
At the listing-day close, plus 10 cents
At the 21-day average, on a pullback
questions.answer: 10 cents over the left-side high
questions.why: 10 cents above the left-side high, the same as most bases. With a market order we do not need the 10 cents.
questions.lesson_line: IBD adds 10 cents to the IPO high. A market order makes it moot.

wrong.At the bottom of the base: That is where the base ends, not where it breaks out.
wrong.At the listing-day close, plus 10 cents: The listing-day close is a level to watch. The buy point is the high on the left side.
wrong.At the 21-day average, on a pullback: An average is a trail and a location check, not the buy point.

questions.q: A textbook IPO base in a Red market is still a buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. In a Red market we hold mostly cash. A Red reading ends the setup before the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Red market: mostly cash. A clean base can wait for a better market.

questions.q: Which floor applies to an IPO base we buy?
choices: No floor while it is a new listing
$10 a share and $20 million a day
$5 a share and $5 million a day
questions.answer: $10 a share and $20 million a day
questions.why: $10 a share and $20 million a day. A new issue gets no pass on liquidity.
questions.lesson_line: Thin, cheap new issues are off the list. The floor is the same for every setup.

wrong.No floor while it is a new listing: A new issue gets no pass. The same liquidity floor applies to every setup.
wrong.$5 a share and $5 million a day: Too thin. Thin, low-priced new issues are a named mistake.

questions.q: Bought at 57.42 with the stop at 56.05. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 61.53. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill. This trade reached it the next day.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.

questions.q: IPO high 54.62, base low 38.63. How deep is the base, in percent?
questions.why: 29.3. Depth runs from the high down to the base's lowest low, divided by the high. BSY sat 29% deep.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high minus low, divided by the high. Read charts in percents.

questions.q: Fill 19.53, stop 18.10. How far under the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 7.3. The stop is 7.3% under the fill. Our stop usually sits within about 3%, so this one is wide and the size must shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent. A wide stop means fewer shares, not a tighter stop.

questions.q: The IPO high is 57.32. What is the most we would pay under the 4% chase limit?
questions.why: 59.61. Add 4% to the buy point. Above that, the stop distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Know the chase limit before the open: 4% over the buy point.

questions.q: Buy at the market?
choices: Yes, heavy volume confirms it
Yes, with a tighter stop
No, it is over 4% past the pivot
questions.answer: No, it is over 4% past the pivot
questions.why: No. 60.10 is more than 4% above 57.32. Heavy volume is a cue, not a license to chase.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% over the pivot you are chasing. Wait for another setup.

wrong.Yes, heavy volume confirms it: Volume is a cue. It does not lift the 4% chase limit.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap. The honest stop stays where it is.

questions.story: A new issue's IPO high is 57.32. It gaps through and trades at 60.10 at 10:20 on heavy volume.

questions.q: On a new issue the base low is the stop.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low. Widening the stop to sit through the base's depth is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: The base low is not the stop. The breakout day's low is.

questions.q: Which volume pattern on the right side of the base is healthy?
choices: Up days heavier than down days
Down days heavier than up days
Equal volume every day
questions.answer: Up days heavier than down days
questions.why: Up days heavier than down days. On the right half, up-close volume exceeds down-close volume.
questions.lesson_line: On the right half of the base, buyers should show up on the green days.

wrong.Down days heavier than up days: That is distribution. Heavy selling on the right side is a warning.
wrong.Equal volume every day: Flat volume says nothing. We look for heavy on up days, light on pullbacks.

questions.q: What is your move?
choices: Buy now with a wide stop
Wait; no buys in the listing week
Buy the close; momentum is proof
questions.answer: Wait; no buys in the listing week
questions.why: Wait. Never buy in the listing week. Wait for the base to emerge; Stockbee says let the flipping phase be over.
questions.lesson_line: A hot debut is not a setup. Wait for the first base.

wrong.Buy the close; momentum is proof: Buying the first heated days is a named mistake. Momentum has no base and no stop.
wrong.Buy now with a wide stop: A wide stop does not fix a buy with no base. Wait for the pivot.

questions.story: A hot IPO lists on Tuesday and rips all day. By Thursday it is up another 20% on huge volume.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Buy at market; new issues run
Wait for it to form its first base
Buy a starter now, add later
questions.answer: Wait for it to form its first base
questions.why: Wait. IBD: let the stock develop some trading history and wait for its first base. A straight run has no pivot and no honest stop.
questions.lesson_line: No base, no trade. The first base is what we wait for.

wrong.Buy a starter now, add later: We do not add. The full size goes in at one price with one stop.
wrong.Buy at market; new issues run: A massive run with no base is a named mistake. Avoid buying a new issue right after one.

questions.story: A stock listed two days ago and has run straight up. A friend says to buy before it gets away.

questions.q: The base averaged 1,200,000 shares a day. How many shares must trade on breakout day for 1.4x?
questions.why: 1,680,000. Multiply the base's average by 1.4. The listing week stays out of that average.
questions.lesson_line: Measure breakout volume against the base's own sessions, not the listing week.

questions.q: What now?
choices: Sell it all; the breakout failed
Sell half; it is back in the base
Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. The stop is the exit. A breach of the pivot back into the base is a warning, not an exit by itself.
questions.lesson_line: A close back inside the base is a warning. Only the stop sells.

wrong.Sell half; it is back in the base: The stop is our exit. Selling half on a warning is not a rule.
wrong.Sell it all; the breakout failed: A warning is not an exit. Wait for the stop or the plan to decide.

questions.story: You bought the IPO-high break at 19.53. Two days later it closes back inside the base, but still above your stop.

questions.q: Which breakout day is the A+ one?
choices: Day A, because it is closer to 1.4x
Day B: the most volume since listing
Neither; volume does not grade it
questions.answer: Day B: the most volume since listing
questions.why: Day B. A+ volume is 2 times the 10-day average or the highest since listing, and IBD wants a close near the highs. Day B closed at the high.
questions.lesson_line: A+ breakouts show the heaviest volume since listing and a close near the high.

wrong.Day A, because it is closer to 1.4x: Day A is acceptable on volume but closes mid-range. Day B shows more demand.
wrong.Neither; volume does not grade it: Volume is a grade cue. A+ shows the heaviest volume and a close near the high.

questions.story: Same base, two breakout days. Day A trades 1.6x the base's volume and closes mid-range. Day B trades the heaviest volume since listing and closes at the high.

questions.q: Buy the breakout today?
choices: No; wait until after the report
Yes, the base is clean and tight
Yes, but at half size, to be safe
questions.answer: No; wait until after the report
questions.why: No. No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. A new issue's first report can come soon after listing, so check the date.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date on a new issue. Inside 3 sessions, wait.

wrong.Yes, the base is clean and tight: A clean base does not lift the earnings rule. A report is a gap risk.
wrong.Yes, but at half size, to be safe: The rule is no new buy in that window, not a smaller one.

questions.story: The base is tight under the IPO high and breaks out this morning. The first quarterly report is in 2 sessions.

questions.q: A stock listed 6 weeks ago rests under its high. Which card applies?
choices: The cup with handle card
The IPO base card
The flat base card
questions.answer: The IPO base card
questions.why: The IPO base card. The listing date decides: an IPO base is a young stock's first rest under its post-listing high inside its first year.
questions.lesson_line: Many IPO bases look like cups. The listing date decides which card applies.

wrong.The cup with handle card: A cup needs a stock with a trading history. A stock listed 6 weeks ago has none.
wrong.The flat base card: A flat base is for a seasoned leader, not a stock listed 6 weeks ago.

questions.q: Which card is it?
choices: Neither; it needs a 200-day
The flat base card
The IPO base card
questions.answer: The IPO base card
questions.why: The IPO base card. The stock is young and this is its first rest under its post-listing high. The shape alone does not decide; the listing date does.
questions.lesson_line: Shape alone does not decide. A young stock's first rest is an IPO base.

wrong.The flat base card: A flat base belongs to a seasoned leader. This stock is three months old.
wrong.Neither; it needs a 200-day: A young listing has no 200-day yet. That does not cancel the setup.

questions.story: A stock listed three months ago rests for 16 sessions, 18% deep, under its post-listing high. It is the first rest, and it looks like a flat base.

questions.q: Which setup is it?
choices: A VCP, shrinking swings
A bull flag after a sharp pole
An IPO base with a grade cue
questions.answer: An IPO base with a grade cue
questions.why: An IPO base with a grade cue. A young listing has no 200-day and one rest; tightening inside an IPO base is a grade cue, not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: Tightening inside an IPO base is a grade cue. It does not change the card.

wrong.A VCP, shrinking swings: A VCP is a seasoned stock with shrinking pullbacks above its long averages. This listing has one rest.
wrong.A bull flag after a sharp pole: A flag follows a sharp pole. This is a rest under the IPO high.

questions.story: A stock listed four months ago rests under its IPO high. The weekly swings inside the rest get smaller each week.

questions.q: Is this a buyable IPO base?
choices: No, a V into the pivot is off
Yes, it is back in the top half
Yes, the dip was shallow
questions.answer: No, a V into the pivot is off
questions.why: No. A V ends the base. It runs from the base low to within 5% of the pivot in 5 sessions or fewer, with no pause. Kedia: that kind of time compression fails often.
questions.lesson_line: A fast V straight into the pivot is not a base. It has no right side.

wrong.Yes, the dip was shallow: The depth is not the issue. The straight V leaves no right side to judge.
wrong.Yes, it is back in the top half: Being back near the top is the problem here: there was no tightening on the way.

questions.story: A new issue drops 25% off its IPO high. Then in four sessions, with no pause, it climbs back within 3% of that high.

questions.q: How do you handle the size?
choices: Fewer shares; size from the stop
Set the stop at the low of the base
Pull the stop in to 3% to keep size
questions.answer: Fewer shares; size from the stop
questions.why: Fewer shares. The size comes from the stop, and a wide honest stop means fewer shares. If it does not fit the risk, skip it.
questions.lesson_line: Never pull the stop in to fit the size. Cut the shares or skip.

wrong.Set the stop at the low of the base: The base low is not our stop, and it is farther still.
wrong.Pull the stop in to 3% to keep size: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap. The honest stop stays.

questions.story: A breakout fills at 19.53. The honest stop is 18.10, which is 7.3% away. Your risk budget is fixed.

questions.q: When do you take the first third?
choices: At the open
Sell the whole position
Wait for a higher price
questions.answer: At the open
questions.why: At the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. 3R was the level here.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past your trim level means take the trim at the open.

wrong.Wait for a higher price: The rule says take it at the open. Waiting turns a plan into a hope.
wrong.Sell the whole position: We trim a third and trail the rest.

questions.story: You bought at 57.42 with the stop at 56.05. Next morning the stock opens at 62.00, above 3R at 61.53.

questions.q: Which backdrop do new issues like best?
choices: A market turning up after a correction
A long, crowded advance
A Red market with strong volume
questions.answer: A market turning up after a correction
questions.why: A market turning up after a correction. That is a cue, not a rule. Be careful when the IPO calendar is crowded late in a long advance.
questions.lesson_line: New issues lead best out of a correction. Be careful when the calendar is crowded.

wrong.A long, crowded advance: Be careful there. A crowded IPO calendar late in a long advance is a warning.
wrong.A Red market with strong volume: Red means mostly cash. New issues are sold first when the market weakens.

questions.q: In our scan, most IPO base breakouts were stopped before reaching 3R.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. 36 of the 57 scan hits were stopped before 3R. It is a probability trade with a quick answer.
questions.lesson_line: Most IPO breakouts stop out first. Size from the stop and keep the losses small.

questions.q: Account 100,000, risk 0.5%, buy 57.42, stop 56.05. How many shares?
questions.why: 364. Divide the dollars at risk by the risk per share and round down. The shares come from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Shares come from the stop: risk in dollars divided by risk per share, rounded down.

questions.q: Which average is the default trail for a fast-moving new issue?
choices: The 200-day
The 50-day
The 10-day
questions.answer: The 10-day
questions.why: The 10-day. IPOs are fast movers, so we sell on a close below the 10-day. A steady mover can use the 21-day.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover: trail the 10-day. Steady mover: trail the 21-day.

wrong.The 50-day: That is too slow for a fast mover. It gives back too much.
wrong.The 200-day: A young listing may not have one, and it is far too slow to trail.

questions.q: What is the plan?
choices: Sell it and free the money
Add more; it is cheap
Hold; the base was clean
questions.answer: Sell it and free the money
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
questions.lesson_line: A trade that does nothing for 10 days is sold. Capital is for working trades.

wrong.Hold; the base was clean: The time stop does not care about the base. Under 1R after 10 days, we sell.
wrong.Add more; it is cheap: We do not add. The full size goes in at one price with one stop.

questions.story: You bought an IPO breakout 10 trading days ago. It has drifted sideways and is up only 0.4R.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Move the stop lower and wait
Take the loss; re-buy on a new trigger
Buy again at once; the base was clean
questions.answer: Take the loss; re-buy on a new trigger
questions.why: Take the loss. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop. MA ran for years afterwards, and the stop was still right.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out on a textbook base is the system working. Re-buy only on a new trigger.

wrong.Buy again at once; the base was clean: A re-buy needs a new trigger, a new stop and every rule again.
wrong.Move the stop lower and wait: The stop never moves down or wider. It is the exit.

questions.story: A textbook IPO base breaks out on 1.6x volume and closes near its high. The next session it falls through your stop.

questions.q: After a stop-out we can buy the same stock again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, with its own stop and every rule. At most 3 tries in a week.
questions.lesson_line: A new buy is a new trade: new trigger, new stop, every rule again.

questions.q: After the first third at 3R, what comes next?
choices: Sell everything at 5R and move on
Add a third at 5R if it acts well
Another third at 5R, then the trail
questions.answer: Another third at 5R, then the trail
questions.why: Another third at 5R, then trail the last third. The stop goes to breakeven by default at the first trim.
questions.lesson_line: Thirds at 3R and 5R, then a trail. Breakeven comes at the first trim.

wrong.Sell everything at 5R and move on: The plan keeps a third on the trail for the big runners.
wrong.Add a third at 5R if it acts well: We do not add to a trade.

questions.q: What do you do with your long?
choices: Add; trends keep going
Hold everything for the 10-day
Sell a big part into the burst
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long is a judgment call, and selling into strength is the plan.
questions.lesson_line: When a new issue goes parabolic, sell a big part into the strength.

wrong.Add; trends keep going: We do not add. A climax is when we sell, not buy.
wrong.Hold everything for the 10-day: The 10-day trail is the floor. A climax run is a reason to sell a big part.

questions.story: Your new-issue long has run 400% in seven weeks. It was up three days running, and today it gaps up again on huge volume.

questions.q: What is the call?
choices: Take half size, it broke out
Pass; it undercut the IPO price
Take it; a shakeout is healthy
questions.answer: Pass; it undercut the IPO price
questions.why: Pass. A base that undercuts the IPO price is off. IBD and MarketSmith India want the base to hold above it. Our SPOT case, a direct listing, undercut its opening price by 18% and its breakout reached 0.0R.
questions.lesson_line: A base that sinks under the IPO price has a hole in its floor.

wrong.Take half size, it broke out: Size is not the fix. The base failed the floor.
wrong.Take it; a shakeout is healthy: This is no shakeout. The base sat under the IPO price for two weeks.

questions.story: A new issue priced its IPO at 20.00 and opened at 21.00. Its IPO high is 23.50. The first base closes under 20.00 for two weeks, with a low of 19.00, before the stock trades through 23.50.

questions.q: Which card judges it now?
choices: No card; skip it, it is too old
The IPO base card, it listed lately
A regular base, on its own rules
questions.answer: A regular base, on its own rules
questions.why: A regular base. The stock is past its first year, so it is judged by its own rules, flat base or cup.
questions.lesson_line: Past the first year, an IPO base turns into a regular base.

wrong.No card; skip it, it is too old: The base can still be good. It just needs the right card.
wrong.The IPO base card, it listed lately: 318 sessions is past a year. The IPO base card has timed out.

questions.story: A clean 3.6-week, 14% shelf under the high breaks out on 2.2x volume. The breakout comes 318 sessions after listing.

questions.q: How strong is this breakout?
choices: Strong; spin-offs run
Strong; the base was tight
Weak; no demand on the day
questions.answer: Weak; no demand on the day
questions.why: Weak. Volume of 0.75x the base's average is below average. IBD wants heavy volume on the breakout day and week. Best was 0.82R.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout on below-average volume has no demand behind it.

wrong.Strong; the base was tight: A tight base helps, but the breakout day still needs buyers.
wrong.Strong; spin-offs run: The listing type does not matter. The volume on the day does.

questions.story: A spin-off listed in June. A 6-week, 10% base at the high breaks out in October on 0.75x the base's average volume.

questions.q: What went wrong?
choices: The stop should have been wider
Nothing; the stop did its job
We should have skipped the breakout
questions.answer: Nothing; the stop did its job
questions.why: Nothing went wrong. The honest stop was 6.7% away and sized for it. The trade reached 0.6R and fell to the stop four sessions later. That is a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: A wide honest stop is sized in shares. When it hits, the loss is the plan.

wrong.The stop should have been wider: Widening the stop is a named mistake. It only grows the loss.
wrong.We should have skipped the breakout: Every rule passed, and the size was set from the stop. Skipping it afterwards is hindsight.

questions.story: MDB: a 20% base on 1.8x volume. The honest stop is 6.7% under the fill. It reaches 0.6R, then falls to the stop four sessions later.

questions.q: What does a Yellow reading change?
choices: Full risk on clean bases
Smaller and fewer positions
Only A+ setups
questions.answer: Smaller and fewer positions
questions.why: Smaller and fewer positions. Yellow is not Green. APTV broke out twice on clean bases in a flat market and stopped out both times.
questions.lesson_line: In a flat market, clean bases still fail. Yellow means smaller and fewer.

wrong.Full risk on clean bases: Full risk is for Green, a market that is working.
wrong.Only A+ setups: That is Orange. Yellow means smaller and fewer, not A+ only.

questions.story: APTV's first base stops out. Months later a second clean base breaks out on 2.8x volume in the same flat market and stops out the next session. Your market reading says Yellow.

questions.q: Was the setup wrong?
choices: No; the loss is planned
Yes; the base was too short
Yes; the stop was too tight
questions.answer: No; the loss is planned
questions.why: No. Every rule passed and the stop was set before the buy. NAVN broke out on 2.1x volume, closed near the high, and fell through the stop the next session.
questions.lesson_line: A clean setup can still lose. The stop is the cost of finding out.

wrong.Yes; the base was too short: A short base is fine for a new issue. The loss is not proof the rule failed.
wrong.Yes; the stop was too tight: The stop was the honest one. Widening it after the fact only grows the loss.

questions.story: NAVN: a 2-week, 7% shelf at the IPO high breaks out on 2.1x volume and closes near its high. Next session it falls through the 4.6% stop.

questions.q: Two IPO bases are otherwise similar. Which one grades higher on depth?
choices: The 12% deep base
The 33% deep base
Neither; depth does not grade
questions.answer: The 12% deep base
questions.why: The 12% deep base. Shallower bases grade higher: under 20% is the A+ version, and 30% to 35% sits down at B-. Grading stays a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Shallower bases grade higher. Under 20% leans A+, 30% to 35% is B-.

wrong.The 33% deep base: That has it backwards. Shallower bases grade higher.
wrong.Neither; depth does not grade: Depth is one of the signs. It helps decide the grade.

questions.story: Two IPO bases are otherwise similar. One is 12% deep. The other is 33% deep.

questions.q: A steady mover late in its first year. Which trail?
choices: The 21-day
The 10-day
The listing-day low
questions.answer: The 21-day
questions.why: The 21-day. SABR was a steady mover late in its first year, and the 21-day trail fit it better than the 10-day.
questions.lesson_line: Steady mover, 21-day trail. Fast mover, 10-day trail.

wrong.The 10-day: That is the default for fast movers. A steady mover gets shaken out of it.
wrong.The listing-day low: That is a level to watch, not a trail.

questions.q: Was the breakout buyable?
choices: Yes, it broke out on volume
Yes, if you use a tight stop
No; too stretched and past 4%
questions.answer: No; too stretched and past 4%
questions.why: No. We skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. A gap this size is also past 4% over the pivot. Skip it and wait for a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: A gap-and-go is not a buy. Skip it and let the next setup come.

wrong.Yes, it broke out on volume: A breakout is the start of the test, not the whole rule. The stretch limit still applies.
wrong.Yes, if you use a tight stop: The stop stays honest. A bigger stop distance shrinks the shares and does not make a stretched entry fine.

questions.story: A new issue gaps up and opens 12% above its IPO high. At the open it is 18% over its 10-day average.

questions.q: Hold through the report?
choices: No; hold only if up 5R
Yes; the stop covers it
Yes; it is a winner
questions.answer: No; hold only if up 5R
questions.why: No. We hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. At 2R, plan to be out before the report.
questions.lesson_line: Hold through a report only when you are up 5R. Otherwise, be out.

wrong.Yes; it is a winner: Being up 2R is not enough. The bar is 5R.
wrong.Yes; the stop covers it: A gap can jump a stop. That is why the rule exists.

questions.story: You hold an IPO winner that is up 2R. Its first report as a public company comes after the close tomorrow.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Take it; the chart is perfect
Take it at half size to be safe
Pass; too thin and too cheap
questions.answer: Pass; too thin and too cheap
questions.why: Pass. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Trading thin, low-priced new issues is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: A perfect chart on a thin stock is still a pass.

wrong.Take it; the chart is perfect: The chart comes after the floor. Thin names are not even watched.
wrong.Take it at half size to be safe: Size does not fix a liquidity failure. The floor is the same for every setup.

questions.story: A new issue trades at 7.40 and averages 3 million dollars a day. Its base and breakout both look perfect.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Add; it is much cheaper than before
Get out; the loss is past 2R
Hold; wait for it to recover
questions.answer: Get out; the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Get out. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop. If the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, we get out.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets 30 minutes. Past 2R, get out.

wrong.Add; it is much cheaper than before: We never add to a trade, least of all one that has gapped through its stop.
wrong.Hold; wait for it to recover: The gap rule sets the new stop at the first 30-minute low. Past 2R, we do not wait.

questions.story: You bought at 57.42 with the stop at 56.05, so 1R is 1.37. The stock gaps down and the first 30-minute low is 52.40. That loss is more than 2R.

questions.q: What does the earnings dip do to the grade?
choices: Nothing; fundamentals are ignored here
It voids the setup and the grade
A miss lowers it; chart comes first
questions.answer: A miss lowers it; chart comes first
questions.why: A miss lowers the grade. We prefer growing sales and earnings, and the chart comes first. It does not void the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Growth is a grade cue. The chart stays the boss.

wrong.Nothing; fundamentals are ignored here: They do matter for the grade. A miss lowers it.
wrong.It voids the setup and the grade: Fundamentals are a preference, not a gate. The chart comes first.

questions.story: A clean IPO base breaks out in a leading group. Its latest quarter shows sales up but earnings down year over year.

questions.q: We have a separate size cut written for new listings.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The rulebook has no rule for new listings. Size comes from the stop and the grade: B- or lower is sized down.
questions.lesson_line: No special IPO size rule. The stop and the grade set the size.

questions.q: A right side with two days of 4% or more in the last 5 sessions is orderly.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The last 5 sessions should hold no two days of 4% or more in either direction. Stockbee uses the same test.
questions.lesson_line: Wide swings on the right side mean the base is not tight yet.

questions.q: Which right side marks the best IPO base?
choices: Wide swings with heavy volume
A fast V into the pivot
Inside days on very low volume
questions.answer: Inside days on very low volume
questions.why: Inside days on very low volume, with weekly ranges under 10%. IBD described CBRE's base as tight trading with weekly ranges under 10%.
questions.lesson_line: The best right side is quiet: inside days, low volume, tight weekly ranges.

wrong.A fast V into the pivot: That is a B- sign. The V leaves no right side to judge.
wrong.Wide swings with heavy volume: That is a loose base, not a tight one.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a breakout. Is this a first rest under the IPO high? Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; a tight rest under the high
Pass; a new issue cannot form a base
Pass; it has no 200-day
questions.answer: Take it; a tight rest under the high
questions.why: Take it. A 6.8-week, 22% deep first base under the IPO high, with the low held above the IPO open. It broke out the next day on 2.2x volume and reached 3R the day after.
questions.lesson_line: Find the IPO high first. Then look for a quiet rest under it.

wrong.Pass; a new issue cannot form a base: IBD says new issues do form bases, short and shallow ones. This is exactly that.
wrong.Pass; it has no 200-day: A young stock has no 200-day yet. The IPO high and the IPO price are its landmarks.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades through its high. Does the base hold above the first day's open?
choices: Take it; the shelf is tight
Pass; the base sank under the first open
Take it; the volume is rising
questions.answer: Pass; the base sank under the first open
questions.why: Pass. The base low 135.51 sat under the IPO open 165.90, an 18% undercut. The breakout reached 0.0R. This is a direct listing and the chart begins on its first day.
questions.lesson_line: Compare the base low with the first day's open before you look at the breakout.

wrong.Take it; the shelf is tight: A tight shelf does not fix a floor that already broke.
wrong.Take it; the volume is rising: Volume is one sign. The base failed the floor first.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Check base, stop and size first
Buy half now, decide the rest later
Buy now before it runs away
questions.answer: Check base, stop and size first
questions.why: Check it yourself. Never take a trade from an alert, a post or a video without your own entry, stop and size. Write the plan before the open.
questions.lesson_line: Someone else's alert is not a plan. Build your own entry, stop and size.

wrong.Buy half now, decide the rest later: Half a gamble is still a gamble. The plan comes first.
wrong.Buy now before it runs away: A buy with no stop and no size is a gamble.

questions.story: A post says a new issue is breaking out right now. You have not looked at its base, its stop or its size.

questions.q: What is your call on the setup?
choices: Pass; Red means mostly cash
Buy it; it has relative strength
Buy a starter position
questions.answer: Pass; Red means mostly cash
questions.why: Pass. In a Red market we hold mostly cash, and a Red reading ends the setup before the trigger. New issues are sold first when the market weakens.
questions.lesson_line: A great setup in a Red market waits. Cash is a position.

wrong.Buy a starter position: A starter in a Red market is still a long. Mostly cash means mostly cash.
wrong.Buy it; it has relative strength: Relative strength does not cancel a Red market. New issues fall hardest.

questions.story: A textbook IPO base is one tick from its pivot. The market reading is Red and the indexes are breaking down.

questions.q: Which base would you rather take?
choices: Neither; volume does not matter here
Base A: selling shakes out weak hands
Base B: heavy volume on up days
questions.answer: Base B: heavy volume on up days
questions.why: Base B. Light volume on the pullbacks and heavy on the up days is the healthy pattern. On the right half, up-day volume should exceed down-day volume.
questions.lesson_line: Two bases can look alike. Volume on the right half tells them apart.

wrong.Neither; volume does not matter here: Volume in the base is a gate on the right half, and it matters.
wrong.Base A: selling shakes out weak hands: Selling on the right half is distribution, not a shakeout.

questions.story: Two IPO bases have the same depth and length. In Base A the right-half down days carry the heavy volume. In Base B the up days do.

questions.q: What does the location tell you?
choices: A good sign; the grade rises
Nothing; the averages do not matter
It is stretched; skip it
questions.answer: A good sign; the grade rises
questions.why: A good sign, so the grade rises. The A+ location is above the IPO AVWAP and the rising 10-day and 21-day.
questions.lesson_line: Above the IPO AVWAP and the rising short averages is the best location.

wrong.It is stretched; skip it: Stretched is measured against the 10-day. Sitting above it is normal.
wrong.Nothing; the averages do not matter: Location is part of the grade. Above all three is the A+ version.

questions.story: A breakout candidate sits above its IPO AVWAP. It is also above its rising 10-day and 21-day averages.

questions.q: Does it change the plan?
choices: Yes; sell everything at 2R
Yes; take a smaller trim at 1R
No; the full plan stands
questions.answer: No; the full plan stands
questions.why: No. The plan is the same: stop under the breakout day's low, thirds at 3R and 5R, trail the rest. There is no special rule for a new issue.
questions.lesson_line: A new issue gets the same plan as any setup. Entry, stop, trim, trail, advance.

wrong.Yes; sell everything at 2R: The trims are thirds at 3R and 5R, then a trail.
wrong.Yes; take a smaller trim at 1R: There is no 1R trim. The first third is at 3R.

questions.story: You buy an IPO base breakout. A friend says new issues need a different exit plan from every other setup.

questions.q: Which card is it?
choices: No card; it is too old
The IPO base card
A regular base card, not the IPO base
questions.answer: A regular base card, not the IPO base
questions.why: A regular base card. The stock listed years ago and is far from its first year, so the IPO base card does not apply.
questions.lesson_line: An old stock gets an old stock's card. Do not force the IPO label.

wrong.The IPO base card: The IPO base card is for a young stock's first rest inside its first year.
wrong.No card; it is too old: Old stocks make bases too. They follow their own cards.
